newsitem.title: USA: Rare U.S. polio case confounds hopes for eradication.
newsitem.headline: Rare U.S. polio case confounds hopes for eradication.

text.p: An unusual case in which the polio virus may have lived in a patient for as long as seven years may complicate efforts to completely eliminate the highly contagious disease, U.S. health officials said on Thursday.

The Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said the case of a teenager who developed polio seven years after he was given the vaccine at age nine raised new questions about the paralytic disease that health officials hope to eradicate worldwide by the year 2000.

"We want to eradicate all forms of polio virus, not only the naturally occurring forms of polio virus, but also vaccine virus, in the end," the CDC's Dr. Roland Sutter said. "We will have to pay more attention to vaccine virus and make sure that we will not have any surprises coming back at us."

The case cited by the CDC involved a teenager who had a weakened immune system. After he was vaccinated, the polio virus replicated and genetically drifted for at least 2-1/2 years and possibly as long as seven years.

"If the seven years is in fact correct, this would represent the longest period of time that a virus has been replicating in a person that we are aware of," Sutter said. "Before, we assumed two to three years."

Government health experts have recommended a shift to use of an inactivated polio virus, because between 1980 and 1994 about 125 people are believed to have contracted polio from the vaccine made from live virus.

The Western Hemisphere was certified as free of indigenous wild poliovirus cases in 1994. Until polio is eradicated worldwide, officials stress the need to continue to vaccinate children in the United States against polio early in their first year of life.

Health officials say the oral polio vaccine should not be given to people with weakened immune systems because they are at increased risk for vaccine-associated paralytic polio. Instead, they should receive the vaccine made from killed virus.
"The whole issue of how and when to stop vaccination has become much more important," Sutter said.
In the case cited by the CDC, the patient hadn't been diagnosed as being immunosuppressed at the time he was given the polio vaccine.
